label: GPT-6 Astra
output:
Dear Nana,

I’ve started this letter a few times now. I get a little way into it, think about you and Aunt Denise sitting in the kitchen, and have to close the laptop. So if Denise has to stop for a minute while she’s reading, tell her I already used up most of the crying and she’s supposed to be the professional.

I wish I were there with you tonight. I wish I could be there tomorrow, carrying things to the car and asking where you want them, then moving them again when you’ve had a better idea. I’m primary on call all week, and I couldn’t find anyone to swap. I know you understand. Everyone has told me it’s fine, and I believe them until I picture that kitchen, and then I wish I were there all over again.

But I don’t want to spend this whole letter apologizing and make you reassure me from Sudbury. You’ve got enough to do without looking after my feelings as well. I’m coming up the weekend of December 5, once this rotation is done. That’s not very far away, and I’m really looking forward to seeing you in your new place.

Before you leave Kathleen Street, though, there are some things I want to say about what that house has meant to me. I don’t think I’ve ever properly told you.

When I think about summers there, I think about the little TV in the kitchen and getting to stay up to watch the Expos or the Jays, as long as I dried the dishes. At the time, I thought this was an excellent arrangement. Looking back, I see that you managed to get the dishes dried by a child who thought they were receiving a special privilege. Very good management. You could have run a company, although I’m not sure a company would have survived your standards for dish towels.

I loved being allowed to stay up with you. I loved being in the kitchen after the day was mostly over, with a game on and something useful to do beside you. I probably thought the baseball was the important part. It wasn’t, really. It was getting that extra time with you.

And I think about the back steps. You with your tea at six in the morning, and me coming out to sit with you. You didn’t talk until your cup was finished. I knew that was the arrangement, too. I love that memory more the older I get. There aren’t many places where you can sit beside somebody without either of you needing to say anything, and feel completely at home.

You gave me that.

You also taught me crib when I was about seven, and then spent the next eight years making absolutely sure I understood that love and mercy at the crib board were two entirely different things. You never once let me win. I’m still impressed by your commitment to beating a small child at cards.

When I finally skunked you at fifteen, you made me a whole pan of butter tarts. I remember the win, obviously. I intend to remember that win for the rest of my life. But I remember the butter tarts just as much. You weren’t about to hand me a victory I hadn’t earned, but once I earned it, you made a fuss. That meant a lot to me.

It’s why I asked for the crib board. I want something we actually used together, something I can keep using. Although I should make clear that asking for the board was not an agreement to stop playing you. You’re not getting out of the rematch that easily.

Fifty-one years is such a long time to live in one house. I’m thirty-four, and I can’t really get my head around all the ordinary days that adds up to. All the meals and dishes and cups of tea. All the people coming through the kitchen. You raised about half our family in there, and the rest of us certainly benefited from it.

When I picture the house, Grandpa Walt is part of it, too. I miss him. I know there’s a lot wrapped up in leaving a place you shared for so long, especially with him gone since 2019. I won’t pretend I know exactly how tonight feels for you. You might feel several different ways before bedtime, and then differently again in the morning.

You’re allowed to be sad about leaving and excited about Elmwood at the same time. You don’t have to choose one feeling to make things easier for the rest of us.

I’ve been trying to find a way to say what that house meant without making this sound like a farewell to you, because it absolutely isn’t. You’ll be on the second floor at Elmwood Terrace, looking out at the parking lot and that big maple, probably discovering very quickly who is worth playing crib with.

And I’m genuinely excited about that part. A place with a crib league seems promising. I hope they understand what they’ve let themselves in for. Perhaps the church ladies should send over a warning before your first game.

I’m proud of you, Nana. I hope that doesn’t sound funny coming from me, but I am. You looked at what you wanted and made this decision yourself. You picked Elmwood. Nobody made you. It takes courage to leave somewhere you’ve lived for fifty-one years, even when you’re looking forward to where you’re going. I admire you for being willing to do it.

I want to hear what you like about it once you’re settled. I want to hear who you’ve met, how the crib is, and what you can see from your window. I want there to be things about it that you enjoy right away, and other things that get better as it starts to feel familiar.

You have always been very good at making sure I’m all right, even from a distance. When I got the job in Toronto, you mailed me a twenty-dollar bill taped inside a card and wrote, “For pizza, you look thin on the computer.” I still think about that. I’d got this grown-up job and moved to Toronto, and you were making sure I had supper money.

Then last Christmas my pager went off during dinner, and you asked whether the internet was broken again and whether I’d fixed it. Now every time we talk, you ask, “Did anything break?”

Honestly, that’s a fairly accurate summary of my job. I could have saved everyone a lot of time explaining site reliability engineering if I’d started with you.

I love that you ask. You don’t need to know every technical detail to care about how my day went. You’ve always found your way into whatever is happening in my life. I’m grateful for that, even when I’m distracted or tired and don’t say it properly.

So tonight, sitting in that kitchen one last time, I hope you know how much of my childhood I’m happy to remember because of you. Thank you for the summers, the late baseball games, the quiet mornings, the butter tarts, and the card games I had to get good enough to win. Thank you for making room for me there.

Denise will have the cuckoo clock and the cedar chest. I’ll have the crib board. And we’ll all still have you to call, to visit, and to tell us what we’re doing wrong when we count our hands.

I love you so much, Nana. I wish I could give you a hug tonight. Please collect one from Denise on my behalf, and I’ll bring my own on December 5.

When I come up that weekend, I want the tour. Show me your room, the maple, and wherever the serious crib players gather. Then we’ll sit down with our board and play our first game at the new place.

Same rules as always. Don’t you dare let me win.

Love you.
